info.text:
Three giant central banks raised rates within nine days in September 2026: the ECB (deposit rate 2.50%), the Fed (3.75%-4.00%) and the Bank of Japan (1.25%, its highest since 1995), while the Bank of England held at 3.75% and China held its loan prime rates. This video explains what central banks do, their mandates and history, how Japan went from negative rates to 1.25%, how a Bank of Japan hike helped rattle markets in August 2024, and how rate moves reach American wallets through mortgages, savings yields and the dollar, with a worked example on a hypothetical $400,000 mortgage at 6.34% versus 7.28% (about $251 more a month). All rates are as of early October 2026. The Fed, ECB, Bank of Japan and Bank of England met again between October 28 and November 5, 2026, after this video's data cutoff; check their latest decisions.

7:40 How it reaches your wallet

Sources: Federal Reserve FOMC statement (Sept. 16, 2026) and H.4.1 (Sept. 24, 2026); ECB monetary policy decisions (Sept. 10, 2026) and weekly financial statement (June 2026); Bank of Japan statement and accounts (2026), CNBC and UPI (Sept. 18, 2026); Bank of England Monetary Policy Summary (Sept. 2026); People's Bank of China LPR announcement via gov.cn and Business Standard (Sept. 2026); Federal Reserve Act Sec. 2A; PBOC Law Art. 3; Freddie Mac PMMS (Oct. 2, 2025 and Oct. 1, 2026); CNBC (10-year yield, Sept. 30, 2026; Nikkei, Aug. 5, 2024; Brent, Sept. 28, 2026); BLS CPI (Aug. 2026); BIS Triennial Survey (2025); nippon.com and Nikkei Asia (BoJ bond holdings); Motley Fool Money (savings APYs, Sept. 30, 2026); Sveriges Riksbank history.

News and education, not financial advice.
